metadata.title: How returns to skills depend on formal qualifications: Evidence from PIAAC

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC 2012 public-use data for 21 countries and restricts the analytic sample to adults aged 16–54 who were not enrolled in full-time education and whose highest formal qualification was obtained in the country of assessment. For the descriptive numeracy gap results (Table 1), the authors explicitly state that survey weights were applied, and they use multiple imputation estimates across the ten PIAAC plausible values. For the multilevel mixed-effects models of occupational status (Table 2), the paper reports random intercepts for countries to account for clustering, but it does not specify a particular weight variable name or replicate-weight method. Overall, the analysis is consistent with complex survey estimation practices for PIAAC (weights + PVs), but the manuscript does not report replicate-weight details, so uncertainty estimation beyond standard errors is not fully transparent.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to PIAAC respondents aged 16–54 who were not enrolled in full-time education at the time of interview, and whose highest formal qualification was obtained in the country of assessment. The study defines less-educated adults as ISCED 0–2 and intermediate-educated adults as ISCED 3–4, excluding respondents with tertiary education (ISCED 5–6). For country comparisons, the authors use 21 countries (excluding Australia, Cyprus, and the Russian Federation due to data-quality/public-file concerns) and further exclude respondents whose highest degree was obtained in a different country than where they took the PIAAC assessment.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes how the labour-market returns to cognitive skills depend on formal qualifications using PIAAC data from 21 countries. The study focuses on less-educated adults (ISCED 0–2) versus intermediate-educated adults (ISCED 3–4), excluding tertiary-educated respondents, and restricts the sample to adults aged 16–54 not enrolled in full-time education. Cognitive skills are measured with PIAAC numeracy (and literacy in robustness notes) using ten plausible values, with survey weights applied and multiple-imputation estimates reported. At the individual level, country-specific multilevel mixed-effects models of occupational status show that numeracy skills partly explain the occupational disadvantage of less-educated adults, but a substantial residual disadvantage remains after controls. At the country level, the remaining disadvantage increases with the aggregate skills gap and with internal homogeneity of the two educational groups, and the skills-to-occupational-status association is weaker among the less educated than among the intermediate group, consistent with employer statistical discrimination and qualification-based screening. The report also notes limitations: PIAAC captures general cognitive skills only, excludes literacy-related non-respondents, and cannot fully test causal mechanisms with the available data.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is treated as a non-ML OECD report/framework-style analysis rather than an empirical machine-learning prediction paper. While the report uses regression and multilevel mixed-effects models with plausible values and survey weights, it does not train or evaluate machine-learning algorithms, so the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty. Consequently, no StructuredFinding rows are produced under the ML-specific schema, and confounder extraction is omitted because the schema is designed for ML predictor/target pipelines rather than regression-based decomposition.
